I’m **Naresh**, a **distributed systems and GPU networking engineer**. I work on the infrastructure that large-scale training and inference run on: kernel networking, RDMA/RoCE, DPDK, SR-IOV, KVM and NCCL. When a 512-GPU job stalls, the cause is usually one bad link, NIC or GPU, while every rank reports the same timeout. I build the infrastructure that finds that one component and gets training back fast, and that moves bytes between GPUs without wasting the hardware.

I also design it to be **secure by construction**. The fastest paths in an AI cluster are the least watched: RDMA bypasses the host kernel, and AI agents now hold the credentials that reach it.

**What I'd own on your team**

- **Make failures attributable.** Turn "all 512 ranks timed out" into "rank 3, `mlx5_2`, bad optic", then take the cheapest recovery that is still safe.
- **Keep the fabric fast under pressure.** RoCE congestion control (PFC, ECN, DCQCN), rail-optimized topologies, KV-cache transport for disaggregated inference.
- **Close the blind spots.** Kernel-bypass traffic, agent credentials, and the checkpoint and model supply chain.

Everything here is **built in public**. A number only appears once it’s measured and linked to its run.

## 🎯 Two problems I work on

<table>
<tr>
<td width="50%" valign="top">

### 🔵 Reliability at scale
**[goodput](https://github.com/nareshns2004/fault-tolerant-training-orchestrator)**: fault attribution & recovery for multi-node training

**Problem.** One bad GPU, NIC, cable or switch port stalls a collective, and *every* rank times out the same way. Stock tooling detects in minutes, attributes nothing, and restarts the whole job.

**Approach.** Fault injection with a ground-truth ledger, NCCL flight-recorder signatures, DCGM and NIC telemetry joined on the topology to name the **culprit rank and component**, then the smallest safe recovery: in-process communicator re-init, single-node replacement, peer in-memory checkpoints.

**Status.** `M1 of 6` · design, interfaces and harness public · no results yet

**Downstream.** goodput's labeled incidents will train two Hugging Face models that plug back in as its classifier: a calibrated, evidence-citing ModernBERT triage tier and a grounded Qwen3 + LoRA root-cause tier ([see below](#hugging-face)). `planned`

</td>
<td width="50%" valign="top">

### 🟠 Efficiency at scale
**[kvwire](https://github.com/nareshns2004/disaggregated-inference-engine)**: RDMA KV-cache transport for disaggregated inference

**Problem.** Prefill is compute-bound and decode is memory-bound. Colocated, they interfere: prefills spike TPOT, decodes spike TTFT.

**Approach.** Split them onto separate GPU pools, and make the part in between fast and safe: a GPUDirect RDMA transport, a Triton KV re-layout kernel (kept only if the data justifies it), and a coordinator that stays correct when the network fails mid-transfer. Plugs into vLLM through its KV-connector interface.

**Status.** `M1` · baselines and hardware ceilings first

</td>
</tr>
</table>

## ⏱️ One timeout, many causes

In NCCL, nearly every hardware fault ends the same way: a watchdog timeout on every rank. The engineering is in the last two columns: naming the one component, then choosing the cheapest recovery that is still safe.

| Fault | What every rank reports | Evidence that names the component | Smallest safe recovery |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPU off the bus (Xid 79) | Watchdog timeout, same collective sequence number | Xid in kernel log / DCGM; the one rank missing from the flight recorder's last completed op | Swap in a spare node, restore from peer in-memory checkpoint |
| Uncorrectable ECC / row-remap failure (Xid 48, 64) | Hang or NaN loss, then timeout | DCGM ECC and row-remap counters on one GPU | Drain node, resume from last checkpoint |
| NVLink fault (Xid 74) | Intra-node collectives stall | Xid 74, NVLink CRC / replay counters | Swap node |
| RoCE link flap or bad optic | Inter-node all-reduce stalls on all ranks | `link_downed`, symbol / CRC errors on one NIC port, IB async events | Communicator re-init once the link recovers; else swap node |
| PFC pause storm | All ranks slow, **no errors anywhere** | Pause counters traced hop by hop to the port that paused first (FIG. 3 below) | Fix the origin (ECN / DCQCN thresholds, isolate port); restarting changes nothing |
| Straggler (thermal / power throttling) | Step-time skew, no timeout | DCGM clock-throttle reasons, per-rank step time | Cordon at the next checkpoint boundary |

<a id="security"></a>

## 🛡️ The fast path is the blind path

An AI agent with a kubeconfig is a remote shell that takes instructions from whatever it reads. One injected sentence in a log line, ticket or web page is enough. No exploit is needed, because **the agent's permissions are the blast radius**. Underneath it, the GPU fabric is where host security sees least: RDMA and GPUDirect bypass the kernel, so host firewalls, eBPF and host IDS never see that traffic, and NCCL has no built-in encryption or peer authentication. In a cluster where model weights are the crown jewels, I treat security as a property of the infrastructure, not a layer added afterwards.

<picture>
  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="assets/security-dark.svg">
  <img alt="FIG. 4, one poisoned input, two outcomes. An untrusted input reaches an AI agent holding infrastructure credentials. Undefended, the injected instruction flows through the agent's identity to the control plane and reaches model weights, checkpoints, training data and the GPU fabric: 4 of 4. Defended, the agent is fooled the same way but a tool boundary, short-lived per-task identity, and signed artifacts with a segmented, encrypted fabric and attested GPUs stop it at the first gate: 0 of 4. Assume the model will be fooled; design so that being fooled is cheap." src="assets/security-light.svg" width="100%">
</picture>

| Layer | What goes wrong | Why AI makes it worse | Control I design for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Agents & tools | Prompt injection steers an agent that can run `kubectl`, `sbatch` or cloud APIs | The agent reads untrusted text all day and acts at machine speed | Read-only tools by default. Mutations go through an allowlisted, audited executor; destructive actions need a human |
| Identity | Long-lived tokens, shared service accounts, ambient admin | One leaked token reaches every node, bucket and checkpoint | Workload identity, short-lived per-task credentials, deny by default |
| Fabric (RDMA / RoCE / NCCL) | Kernel bypass hides traffic from host controls. Collectives cross the fabric in plaintext. A leaked `rkey` grants remote memory access | Gradients, activations and KV cache are the model, in transit | Per-tenant isolation (IB partition keys, VRF per tenant), scoped and revocable memory windows, inline MACsec/IPsec on NICs that offload it, telemetry at the NIC/DPU because the host can't see it |
| Multi-tenant inference | Shared prefix caches leak prompts through timing. GPU memory outlives the job | Serving is multi-tenant by default | Per-tenant cache isolation, scrub on reassignment, MIG or confidential computing (Hopper/Blackwell CC mode) where the threat model needs it |
| Artifacts | Pickled checkpoints run code on load. Unsigned weights and datasets | One tampered checkpoint is restored onto every replica | `safetensors` / `weights_only=True`, signed and hashed checkpoints, dataset provenance |
| My own tooling | goodput's RCA model is itself an agent touching production | Same risk as above, on the infrastructure itself | It **recommends, never acts**: it sees read-only evidence, and recovery runs only through goodput's allowlisted executor `planned` |

<a id="hugging-face"></a>

## 🤗 On Hugging Face: learning that table from ground truth

goodput's fault injector knows exactly what it broke, so every incident it produces is labeled by construction. Those incidents become a public benchmark and two models that plug back into goodput as its classifier, and have to beat its hand-written rules to earn the slot. Models live on **[huggingface.co/nareshns2004](https://huggingface.co/nareshns2004)**.

| Artifact | What it does | Stage |
|---|---|---|
| `infra-failure-bench` · dataset | Multi-host incident windows with root cause, culprit and evidence lines. Test splits hold out cluster topologies, cascades (root ≠ loudest symptom) and real incidents | design · awaiting goodput export |
| `infra-triage-modernbert` | Fast tier: root-cause class, the lines that prove it, calibrated resolve-or-escalate; milliseconds on CPU via ONNX | design |
| [`qwen3-nccl-rca-lora`](https://huggingface.co/nareshns2004/qwen3-nccl-rca-lora) | Slow tier: grounded RCA naming culprit, causal chain and cited lines; GRPO on rewards a script can check (citations exist, category and culprit match the ledger) | model card (no weights yet) |

<a id="runnable"></a>

## 🛠️ Runnable today

- **[nicprof](https://github.com/nareshns2004/ai-nic-performance-profiler)**: which NIC counter explains which millisecond of training step time. Aligns RDMA/ethtool/SR-IOV counters to each rank’s steps and traces PFC pause back to its origin, so a *victim* port isn’t blamed. `nicprof demo` · 69 tests
- **[kptk](https://github.com/nareshns2004/kernel-performance-toolkit)**: explains *why* a Linux workload is slow from kernel evidence: run-queue delay, NUMA locality, THP fallback, and `perf_event_open(2)` called directly. Standard library only · 43 tests

  <source media="(prefers-color-scheme: dark)" srcset="assets/pfc-dark.svg">
  <img alt="FIG. 3, PFC pause propagation. Hosts H0 to H3 send incast traffic through leaf A, a spine and leaf B to one receiver; H4 sends an unrelated flow to R2. Leaf B's egress queue toward the incast receiver fills and PFC pause frames propagate upstream hop by hop to every host. H4's flow stalls although it never touches the congested port: it is a victim. The origin is the leaf B egress port, which nicprof finds by following pause counters back hop by hop." src="assets/pfc-light.svg" width="100%">
